content: Periodinanes are chemical compounds that contain hypervalent iodine atoms. These iodine atoms are considered hypervalent because they possess more than the eight valence electrons typically required by the octet rule. When iodine is coordinated with a monodentate electronegative ligand, such as chlorine, the resulting iodine compounds can exhibit an oxidation state of +3 (iodine(III), also referred to as λ³-iodanes) or +5 (iodine(V), also referred to as λ⁵-iodanes). In its elemental state, iodine has seven valence electrons. In λ³-iodanes, three additional electrons are donated by the ligands, resulting in a decet structure (10 valence electrons). In λ⁵-iodanes, the structure is even more electron-rich, forming a dodecet (12 valence electrons). For comparison, a typical iodine compound like iodobenzene adheres to the octet rule, with eight valence electrons. To form hypervalent iodine compounds, iodine undergoes oxidation, first losing three electrons and then five electrons. The ligands compensate for this electron loss by donating electron pairs, forming coordinate covalent bonds. These ligands contribute a total of six or ten electrons back to the iodine atom. The L-I-N notation is used to describe these compounds, where L represents the number of electrons donated by the ligands, and N represents the number of ligands. This concept was introduced by J. Musher in 1969. To accommodate the excess electrons in hypervalent compounds, the 3-center-4-electron bond model was proposed, analogous to the 3-center-2-electron bond observed in electron-deficient compounds. In iodine(III) compounds, one such bond exists, while iodine(V) compounds contain two of these bonds. The first hypervalent iodine compound, dichloroiodobenzene (C₆H₅Cl₂I), was synthesized in 1886 by the German chemist C. Willgerodt. This was achieved by passing chlorine gas through iodobenzene in a cooled chloroform solution. λ³-iodanes, such as diarylchloroiodanes, exhibit a pseudotrigonal bipyramidal geometry. In this structure, the apical positions are occupied by a phenyl group and a chlorine atom, while the equatorial positions are occupied by another phenyl group and two lone pairs of electrons. λ⁵-iodanes, such as the Dess-Martin periodinane, have a square pyramidal geometry, with four heteroatoms in the basal positions and one apical phenyl group. Classical organic methods exist for preparing hypervalent iodine compounds. For example, iodosobenzene diacetate can be synthesized from peracetic acid and acetic acid. A related compound, phenyl iodine bis(trifluoroacetate) (PIFA), is derived from trifluoroacetic acid. Iodosobenzene diacetate can be hydrolyzed with water to form iodoxybenzene (iodylbenzene, C₆H₅O₂I), a compound first prepared by Willgerodt through the disproportionation of iodosylbenzene under steam distillation. Iodoxybenzene is a known oxidizing agent. Alternatively, iodosobenzene diacetate can be hydrolyzed with sodium hydroxide to form iodosylbenzene, which is a polymer with the molecular formula (C₆H₅OI)ₙ. Iodosylbenzene is widely used in organic oxidation reactions. The Dess-Martin periodinane, introduced in 1983, is a powerful oxidizing agent and an improvement over the IBX acid, which was first synthesized in 1893. IBX acid is prepared from 2-iodobenzoic acid, potassium bromate, and sulfuric acid. While IBX acid is insoluble in most solvents, the Dess-Martin reagent, prepared by reacting IBX acid with acetic anhydride, is highly soluble. The oxidation mechanism of these reagents typically involves a ligand exchange reaction followed by a reductive elimination step. The primary application of hypervalent iodine compounds is as oxidizing agents, often replacing toxic heavy metal-based reagents. Current research focuses on their use in carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bond-forming reactions. For instance, in one study, an intramolecular C-N coupling reaction of an alkoxyhydroxylamine with its anisole group was achieved using a catalytic amount of aryl iodide in trifluoroethanol. In this reaction, the periodinane intermediate (denoted as intermediate A) is formed by oxidizing the aryl iodide with the sacrificial catalyst mCPBA. This intermediate then converts the hydroxylamine group into a nitrenium ion (denoted as intermediate B), which acts as the electrophile in an ipso addition to the aromatic ring, ultimately forming a lactam with an enone group.
